An equation written with the names of the reactants and products instead of their chemical formulas.
An insoluble solid that separates out of a solution during a chemical reaction.
The breaking up of a compound into simpler substances when it is heated.
The breaking up of a compound into simpler substances by passing an electric current through it.
The breaking up of a compound into simpler substances when it is exposed to light.
An acid obtained from minerals of the earth rather than from living things, such as hydrochloric, sulphuric or nitric acid.
An acid produced by plants or animals, such as citric acid, acetic acid or lactic acid.
Adding water to concentrated acid slowly and with stirring, while the mixture warms because the process is exothermic.
An oxide, usually of a metal, that reacts with an acid to give a salt and water.
An oxide, usually of a non-metal, that reacts with a base to give a salt and water.
A mild base taken to neutralise the excess acid in the stomach and relieve indigestion.
The electrolysis of brine, in which sodium chloride solution gives sodium hydroxide along with chlorine at the anode and hydrogen at the cathode.
A salt formed by a strong acid and a strong base, whose solution in water has a pH close to seven.
A salt whose solution in water turns blue litmus red, formed when a strong acid is only partly neutralised.
The shine on the freshly cut surface of a metal, caused by the way it reflects light.
The tendency of a substance to break into pieces rather than bend when it is struck, which is typical of non-metals.
A process in which a clean aluminium article is made the anode and electrolysed so that a thicker protective oxide layer forms on it.
The set of operations by which a metal is obtained from its ore and then purified.
The removal of as much of the gangue as possible from the mined ore before it is heated.
A substance added during smelting that combines with the gangue to form a fusible slag which can be removed.
The fusible mass formed when the flux reacts with the gangue, which floats on the molten metal and is drawn off.
The purification of a metal in which the impure metal is the anode, a thin strip of the pure metal is the cathode, and a salt of the metal is the electrolyte.
The insoluble impurities that settle below the anode during the electrolytic refining of a metal.
The reduction of a metal oxide to the free metal by heating it strongly with a reducing agent such as coke.
A compound made up of ions held together by strong electrostatic forces, formed by the complete transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal.
Another name for an ionic bond, emphasising that it is formed by the transfer of valence electrons.
A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses one or more electrons.
A negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains one or more electrons.
The replacement of a less reactive metal in its salt solution by a more reactive metal, which is how the reactivity series is confirmed.
An alloy of aluminium with copper, magnesium and manganese, which is light and strong and is used in aircraft bodies.
An alloy of iron with chromium, nickel and a little carbon, which resists corrosion and is used for cutlery and surgical instruments.
An alloy of lead and tin with a low melting point, used for joining electrical wires.
A compound whose atoms are joined by shared pairs of electrons, and which therefore has no ions to conduct a current.
A representation of a molecule in which only the valence electrons of each atom are shown as dots around its symbol.
One of two or more different physical forms of the same element, such as diamond, graphite and fullerene for carbon.
An atom other than carbon or hydrogen in the chain of an organic compound, which along with the functional group gives the compound its properties.
An organic compound containing a hydroxyl group attached to a carbon chain, named with the suffix -ol.
An organic compound containing a -CHO group at the end of a carbon chain, named with the suffix -al.
An organic compound in which a carbonyl group is attached to two carbon atoms, named with the suffix -one.
An organic compound containing a -COOH group, named with the suffix -oic acid and weakly acidic in water.
A saturated hydrocarbon in which every carbon-carbon bond is single, following the general formula CnH2n+2.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing one carbon-carbon double bond, following the general formula CnH2n.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing one carbon-carbon triple bond, following the general formula CnH2n-2.
The systematic name of a compound, built from a root word for the length of the carbon chain, a prefix for any substituent and a suffix for the functional group.
A way of writing a compound that shows how its atoms are bonded to one another, rather than only how many of each there are.
Any one member of a homologous series, differing from the next by a CH2 unit and by fourteen units of molecular mass.
A reaction in which atoms are added to an unsaturated compound across its double or triple bond, converting it into a saturated one.
A reaction in which one atom or group in a saturated compound is replaced by another, such as hydrogen being replaced by chlorine in sunlight.
The burning of a substance in air or oxygen with the release of heat and light.
The burning of a carbon compound in enough air to give only carbon dioxide and water, with a clean blue flame.
A sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid, whose molecule has a water-repelling hydrocarbon tail and a water-attracting ionic head.
The long hydrocarbon tail of a soap molecule, which repels water and attaches to oil and grease.
The ionic end of a soap molecule, which dissolves in water and faces outward in a micelle.
The insoluble calcium or magnesium salt that soap forms in hard water, which settles as a sticky deposit and wastes the soap.
Water that contains salts of calcium and magnesium, so that soap does not lather in it until those salts are removed.
